3:story-discussion.why: Bringing notes and a question to a group talk and answering with a reason from the story is «listen actively, ask relevant questions to clarify information, and make pertinent comments»; taking turns in a group of four with sentence starters for adding on, agreeing and disagreeing is «work collaboratively with others by following agreed-upon rules, norms, and protocols».

2:character-challenge.why: Naming the problem of a story, what the character does about it and what happens because of it is «describe and understand plot elements, including the main events, the conflict, and the resolution»; telling how the character feels, with the sentence that shows it, is «describe the main character's internal and external traits».

2:fable-lesson.why: Retelling a fable by its beginning, middle and end is «retell and paraphrase texts in ways that maintain meaning and logical order»; choosing or writing its lesson with the events that show it is «discuss topics and determine theme using text evidence with adult assistance».

1:story-key-details.why: Answering a question about a story and underlining the sentence that tells the answer is «use text evidence to support an appropriate response».

1:characters-setting-events.why: Naming where a story takes place is «describe the setting»; choosing and writing the big thing that happens is «describe plot elements, including the main events»; naming the two characters and what kind of animal each is leads toward «describe the main characters and the reasons for their actions» (the reasons are not asked on these pages).

1:retell-and-lesson.why: Putting three sentences in order and writing the beginning, the middle and the end is «retell texts in ways that maintain meaning»; choosing or writing the lesson of the story is «discuss topics and determine theme using text evidence with adult assistance».

1:feeling-and-sense-words.why: Finding the words of a story that tell a feeling or what is seen, heard, tasted or touched, and naming the sense each speaks to, is «discuss how the author uses words that help the reader visualize».

1:who-tells-the-story.why: Telling the narrator's sentences from the words a character speaks is a first step toward «listen to and experience first- and third-person texts»: the stories are told in the third person, and the children hear who tells and who speaks.

K:story-who-where.why: Circling, drawing and naming the animal a story is about is «identify and describe the main characters»; circling, drawing and naming the place is «describe the setting»; choosing and drawing one big thing that happens is a first step toward «describe the elements of plot development, including the main events, the problem, and the resolution».

K:retell-beginning-middle-end.why: Putting three pictures of a story in order, drawing its beginning, middle and end and telling it with First, Then, At the end is «retell texts in ways that maintain meaning».

K:story-questions.why: Circling the picture that answers a question about a story is «provide an oral, pictorial, or written response to a text»; drawing or telling a question of the child's own is «generate questions about text before, during, and after reading».

K:pictures-and-words.why: Drawing a line from each part of a story to its picture, and drawing the picture that is missing, is «interact with sources in meaningful ways such as illustrating or writing»; seeing that each picture shows what its words tell leads toward «discuss with adult assistance the author's use of print and graphic features».

1:silent-e.why: Reading and spelling one-syllable words with a silent e (cap, cape) is «decoding words with closed syllables; open syllables; VCe syllables; vowel teams, including vowel digraphs and diphthongs; and r-controlled syllables».

1:long-a-ai-ay.why: Reading and spelling one-syllable words with the vowel teams ai and ay is «decoding words with closed syllables; open syllables; VCe syllables; vowel teams, including vowel digraphs and diphthongs; and r-controlled syllables».

1:long-e-ee-ea.why: Reading and spelling one-syllable words with the vowel teams ee and ea is «decoding words with closed syllables; open syllables; VCe syllables; vowel teams, including vowel digraphs and diphthongs; and r-controlled syllables».

1:long-o-oa-ow.why: Reading and spelling one-syllable words with the vowel teams oa and ow is «decoding words with closed syllables; open syllables; VCe syllables; vowel teams, including vowel digraphs and diphthongs; and r-controlled syllables».

1:ck-ng-wh.why: Reading words with ck, ng, and wh is «decoding words with initial and final consonant blends, digraphs, and trigraphs»; writing them is «spelling words with initial and final consonant blends, digraphs, and trigraphs».

1:blends-start.why: Reading words that start with a blend (stop, flag, trip) is «decoding words with initial and final consonant blends, digraphs, and trigraphs»; writing them is «spelling words with initial and final consonant blends, digraphs, and trigraphs».

1:blends-end.why: Reading words that end in a blend (hand, lamp, nest, sink) is «decoding words with initial and final consonant blends, digraphs, and trigraphs»; writing them is «spelling words with initial and final consonant blends, digraphs, and trigraphs».

K:naming-and-action-words.why: Texas states grammar and conventions inside the editing expectation of kindergarten; telling an action word from a naming word and finding it in a sentence is the convention «verbs», and knowing a naming word prepares «singular and plural nouns».

K:capital-letter.why: Texas states grammar and conventions inside the editing expectation of kindergarten; finding and writing the capital at the start of a sentence is «capitalization of the first letter in a sentence and name» (the pages use no names).

K:period-or-question-mark.why: Texas states grammar and conventions inside the editing expectation of kindergarten; ending a telling sentence with a period is «punctuation marks at the end of declarative sentences»; the question mark of an asking sentence goes one step further than the Texas kindergarten wording.

K:make-the-sentence-longer.why: Texas states grammar and conventions inside the editing expectation of kindergarten; saying a whole sentence about a picture and making it longer is the convention «complete sentences».

3:maps-diagrams-photos.why: Reading a map or a diagram together with the words of an informational text, and saying which of the two gave an answer, uses «features such as sections, tables, graphs, timelines, bullets, numbers, and bold and italicized font to support understanding»; it prepares «explain the author's use of print and graphic features to achieve specific purposes».

K:place-words.why: Texas states grammar and conventions inside the editing expectation of kindergarten; choosing and using in, on top of, under, next to and the other place words in a sentence is the convention «prepositions».

1:long-or-short-vowel.why: Saying a one-syllable word and marking its vowel sound long or short is «distinguishing between long and short vowel sounds in one-syllable words».

2:short-or-long-vowel.why: Sorting one-syllable words by a short or a long vowel is «distinguishing between long and short vowel sounds in one-syllable and multi-syllable words»; reading them is «decoding words with short, long, or variant vowels, trigraphs, and blends».

2:vowel-teams-long-a-e-o.why: Reading words with ai, ay, ee, ea, oa, and ow is «decoding words with short, long, or variant vowels, trigraphs, and blends»; choosing and writing the team is «spelling one-syllable and multisyllabic words with closed syllables; open syllables; VCe syllables; vowel teams, including digraphs and diphthongs; r-controlled syllables; and final stable syllables».

2:vowel-sounds-oo-ou-ow-oi-oy.why: Reading words with oo, ou, ow, oi, and oy is «decoding words with short, long, or variant vowels, trigraphs, and blends» (the variant vowels); writing them is «spelling one-syllable and multisyllabic words with closed syllables; open syllables; VCe syllables; vowel teams, including digraphs and diphthongs; r-controlled syllables; and final stable syllables» (the diphthongs).

2:bossy-r-ar-or.why: Reading and writing one-syllable words with ar and or is «spelling one-syllable and multisyllabic words with closed syllables; open syllables; VCe syllables; vowel teams, including digraphs and diphthongs; r-controlled syllables; and final stable syllables» (the r-controlled syllables); it prepares «decoding multisyllabic words with closed syllables; open syllables; VCe syllables; vowel teams, including digraphs and diphthongs; r-controlled syllables; and final stable syllables».

2:er-ir-ur.why: Reading words with er, ir, and ur and checking their spelling is «spelling one-syllable and multisyllabic words with closed syllables; open syllables; VCe syllables; vowel teams, including digraphs and diphthongs; r-controlled syllables; and final stable syllables» (the r-controlled syllables); it prepares «decoding multisyllabic words with closed syllables; open syllables; VCe syllables; vowel teams, including digraphs and diphthongs; r-controlled syllables; and final stable syllables».

2:long-vowels-two-syllable-words.why: Splitting and reading two-syllable words with a vowel team, a silent e, or an open syllable is «decoding multisyllabic words with closed syllables; open syllables; VCe syllables; vowel teams, including digraphs and diphthongs; r-controlled syllables; and final stable syllables»; it prepares «decoding words using knowledge of syllable division patterns such as VCCV, VCV, and VCCCV».

2:tricky-words-could-would-should.why: Reading and writing could, would, should, because, and friend by mapping their sounds and learning the tricky part is «identifying and reading high-frequency words from a research-based list».

K:short-a-i.why: Saying the short sounds of a and i is «identifying and matching the common sounds that letters represent»; reading the words is «using letter-sound relationships to decode, including VC, CVC, CCVC, and CVCC words»; writing the vowel and the word is «spelling words with VC, CVC, and CCVC».

K:short-o-u-e.why: Saying the short sounds of o, u, and e is «identifying and matching the common sounds that letters represent»; reading the words is «using letter-sound relationships to decode, including VC, CVC, CCVC, and CVCC words»; writing the vowel and the word is «spelling words with VC, CVC, and CCVC».

K:change-one-sound.why: A ladder on which each step changes one sound of the word above is «recognizing that new words are created when letters are changed, added, or deleted such as it - pit - tip - tap»; the child writes each new word: «spelling words with VC, CVC, and CCVC».

K:words-one-letter-apart.why: Reading two words that differ in one letter and choosing the one for the picture is «using letter-sound relationships to decode, including VC, CVC, CCVC, and CVCC words»; it prepares «recognizing that new words are created when letters are changed, added, or deleted».

1:capitals-names-days-months.why: Texas asks first graders for «capitalization for the beginning of sentences and the pronoun "I"»; capitals for names, days and months go one step further, and a name with its capital is a proper noun: «singular, plural, common, and proper nouns».

1:joining-words.why: Texas names no joining words in Grade 1; joining two complete sentences with and, but, so or because builds on «complete sentences with subject-verb agreement».

1:verb-tense.why: Writing the past and the present form of a verb is «past and present verb tense» (the future with will goes one step further); yesterday, today and tomorrow are «adverbs that convey time».

2:prefixes-un-re.why: Building and explaining words with un- and re- is «identify the meaning of and use words with affixes un-, re-, -ly, -er, and -est»; reading them is «decoding words with prefixes, including un-, re-, and dis-».

2:suffixes-ful-less-ly.why: Texas names -ly among the affixes of Grade 2: «identify the meaning of and use words with affixes un-, re-, -ly, -er, and -est»; -ful and -less are taught the same way and go one step further.

2:apostrophes.why: Writing contractions with their apostrophe is «end punctuation, apostrophes in contractions»; reading and spelling them is «decoding compound words, contractions» and «spelling compound words, contractions». The owner with an apostrophe and s is not named in the Texas wording of Grade 2.

1:compound-and-two-part-words.why: Reading a compound word as two small words is «using knowledge of base words to decode common compound words and contractions»; splitting rab | bit and nap | kin into two closed syllables is «decoding words with closed syllables».

1:tricky-words-said-was-of-could.why: Reading said, was, of and could is «identifying and reading at least 100 high-frequency words from a research-based list»; writing them with their tricky part is «spelling high-frequency words from a research-based list».

3:closed-open-syllables.why: Marking each syllable closed or open and reading it is «decoding multisyllabic words with closed syllables; open syllables; VCe syllables; vowel teams, including digraphs and diphthongs; r-controlled syllables; and final stable syllables»; splitting rab | bit, ro | bot and cam | el is «decoding words using knowledge of syllable division patterns such as VCCV, VCV, and VCCCV».

3:syllable-types-e-team-le.why: Typing each syllable of a long word (closed, open, silent e, vowel team, consonant-le) and reading the word is «decoding multisyllabic words with closed syllables; open syllables; VCe syllables; vowel teams, including digraphs and diphthongs; r-controlled syllables; and final stable syllables» (consonant-le is the final stable syllable); building the words prepares their spelling.

3:suffixes-able-ment-ness-ful-less.why: Reading words with -able, -ment, -ness, -ful and -less, with a dropped e or a y changed to i, is «decoding words using knowledge of suffixes, including how they can change base words such as dropping e, changing y to i»; saying what the word means is «identify the meaning of and use words with affixes such as ... -ness, -y, and -ful».

3:tricky-words-enough-though-ocean.why: Reading and writing enough, though and ocean with their tricky part is «identifying and reading high-frequency words from a research-based list»; sorting ough words by sound is «decoding multisyllabic words with multiple sound-spelling patterns such as eigh, ough, and en».

3:joining-words.why: Joining two sentences with and, but, or, so is «coordinating conjunctions to form compound subjects, predicates, and sentences»; the comma written before the joining word is «commas in compound sentences». Because, when, if, after and before go one step further than the Texas wording of Grade 3.

3:simple-compound-complex.why: Telling a simple from a compound sentence and writing both is «complete simple and compound sentences with subject-verb agreement»; the comma of the compound sentence is «commas in compound sentences». The complex sentence goes one step further than the Texas wording of Grade 3.

3:comparing-adjectives-adverbs.why: Forming and choosing taller, tallest, more careful, better and best is «adjectives, including their comparative and superlative forms»; comparing how something is done (more carefully, fastest) uses «adverbs that convey time and adverbs that convey manner».

3:possessive-nouns.why: Writing the bee's hive, the bees' hive and the children's coats is «punctuation marks, including apostrophes in contractions and possessives»; telling a possessive from a plain plural rests on «singular, plural, common, and proper nouns».

3:capitals-in-titles.why: Texas names «capitalization of official titles of people, holidays, and geographical names and places» in Grade 3; capitals in the titles of books and stories apply the same convention to a title.

1:words-by-category.why: Sorting words into birds, fish and insects and naming the category of a word is «identify and use words that name actions, directions, positions, sequences, categories, and locations». Defining a word by its category and one attribute goes one step further than the Texas wording.

1:endings-s-ed-ing.why: Reading helps, helped and helping is «decoding words with inflectional endings, including -ed, -s, and -es»; choosing the ending a sentence needs is «identify the meaning of words with the affixes -s, -ed, and -ing».

3:context-clues.why: Finding the clue in the sentence or in the next sentence and saying what the new word means is «use context within and beyond a sentence to determine the meaning of unfamiliar words and multiple-meaning words».

3:dictionary-glossary.why: Finding a word by its guide words, reading its part of speech and choosing the meaning a sentence uses is «use print or digital resources to determine meaning, syllabication, and pronunciation»; the pages work with meaning and spelling, not with syllables and pronunciation.

3:parts-of-speech.why: Texas names the parts of speech in the conventions a third grader edits for: «singular, plural, common, and proper nouns», «adjectives, including their comparative and superlative forms», «adverbs that convey time and adverbs that convey manner» and «pronouns, including subjective, objective, and possessive cases». Sorting words by their job and labeling each word of a sentence teaches what these words are and do.

3:plural-nouns.why: Writing and choosing the plural of a noun is «singular, plural, common, and proper nouns»; adding -es and changing y to i before it is «spelling words using knowledge of suffixes, including how they can change base words such as dropping e, changing y to i, and doubling final consonants».

3:past-tense-verbs.why: Writing the past form of a verb and rewriting a story in the past is «past, present, and future verb tense»; dropping e, doubling the last consonant and changing y to i before -ed is «spelling words using knowledge of suffixes, including how they can change base words such as dropping e, changing y to i, and doubling final consonants».

3:subject-verb-agreement.why: Choosing the verb that agrees with one subject, with two subjects joined by and, and after There is «complete simple and compound sentences with subject-verb agreement». A pronoun that agrees in number with its noun prepares «pronouns, including subjective, objective, and possessive cases», which asks for the case of the pronoun.

2:words-in-real-life.why: Texas has no Grade 2 row for the real-life connections between words and their use. Naming real things that are spicy, juicy or noisy builds the describing words a second grader then uses and edits for: «adjectives, including articles».

2:adjective-or-adverb.why: Choosing the adjective that tells about a noun is «adjectives, including articles». Texas names «adverbs that convey time and adverbs that convey place» in Grade 2; the adverbs of this lesson tell HOW something is done (quickly, bravely), which Texas names in Grade 3 (adverbs that convey manner).

K:book-parts.why: Telling the front cover, the title page and the back cover apart and making a cover and a title page of one's own is «identifying the front cover, back cover, and title page of a book».

K:left-to-right.why: Marking where reading starts and stops, drawing the arrow under each line and back to the next line, and numbering lines and pages is «knowing that reading moves from top to bottom and left to right with return sweep»; holding a book and turning its pages is done with a real book, as the note says.

K:spoken-written-words.why: Circling the word among a letter, a digit and a scribble is «recognizing the difference between a letter and a printed word»; putting one dot under each word of a sentence the teacher says is «recognizing word boundaries».

K:spaces-between-words.why: Drawing a line in each space, counting the words of a sentence, and gluing or copying words with finger spaces is «recognizing that sentences are comprised of words separated by spaces and recognizing word boundaries».

3:opinion-and-reasons.why: Checking fact or opinion for each sentence is «distinguishing facts from opinion»; underlining the opinion of a piece is «identifying the claim»; filling the planner (opinion, reasons with examples, conclusion) is «plan a first draft ... using a range of strategies such as ... mapping»; the plan prepares the opinion essay of «compose argumentative texts, including opinion essays».

3:linking-words.why: Drafting the piece from introduction to conclusion is «compose argumentative texts, including opinion essays, using genre characteristics and craft»; giving each reason an example and joining them with because, since, therefore and for example is «developing an engaging idea with relevant details»; the introduction and the conclusion boxes of the draft prepare «organizing with purposeful structure, including an introduction and a conclusion».

3:concluding-statement.why: Choosing the conclusion of a piece (not a new reason, not the opinion copied word for word) and writing conclusions of one's own is the conclusion part of «organizing with purposeful structure, including an introduction and a conclusion».

3:revise-and-edit.why: Crossing out the sentence that does not belong, adding a sentence with a linking word after a partner's comment and fixing capitals, end marks and commas is «revise drafts ... by adding, deleting, combining, and rearranging ideas for coherence and clarity»; the edit rows of 3.11.D name other conventions (verb tense, nouns, adjectives) and are not claimed.

3:plan-a-story.why: Filling the story planner beside a story mountain is «plan a first draft ... using a range of strategies such as ... mapping»; naming the problem of a story beginning and planning events and an ending prepares «analyze plot elements, including the sequence of events, the conflict, and the resolution»; telling a narrator who says I from one who is not in the story prepares «first- or third-person point of view»; the plan prepares the story of «compose literary texts, including personal narratives».

3:dialogue-and-description.why: Writing what characters say with quotation marks and showing a feeling with an action or a thought instead of naming it is the craft of «compose literary texts ... using genre characteristics and craft» and is «developing an engaging idea with relevant details»; the Grade 3 edit rows of 3.11.D do not name quotation marks, so none is claimed.

3:time-words-in-stories.why: Drafting the planned story is «compose literary texts, including personal narratives»; writing it under Beginning, Middle and Ending with an ending that solves the problem is «organizing with purposeful structure, including an introduction and a conclusion»; choosing first, next, later that day and finally for the order of events prepares «adverbs that convey time».

3:words-for-effect.why: Replacing tired words with exact ones in a paragraph and in the child's own sentences is «revise drafts to improve sentence structure and word choice».

3:take-notes-and-sort.why: Choosing and writing a note of a few words for a sentence of a source and sorting notes under headings is «interact with sources in meaningful ways such as notetaking»; taking the notes a heading needs from one and from two printed sources is «identify and gather relevant information from a variety of sources».

3:introduce-and-group.why: Filling the planner (an introduction, three headings with their notes, a concluding sentence) is «plan a first draft ... using a range of strategies such as ... mapping»; choosing and writing the introduction that covers every group of notes is the introduction part of «organizing with purposeful structure, including an introduction and a conclusion»; the plan prepares «compose informational texts ... using a clear central idea».

3:facts-definitions-details.why: Drafting the planned piece in three parts is «compose informational texts, including brief compositions that convey information about a topic»; adding a definition and details to each fact is «developing an engaging idea with relevant details»; the concluding sentence is the conclusion part of «organizing with purposeful structure, including an introduction and a conclusion».

3:short-research-report.why: Filling the note chart from Source A and Source B for a research question is «identify and gather relevant information from a variety of sources»; writing the report from those notes is «demonstrate understanding of information gathered» and «compose informational texts»; writing the research question on Level 3 prepares «generate questions on a topic for formal and informal inquiry», and the line that names both sources prepares «create a works cited page».

2:plan-an-opinion.why: Filling the planner (an opinion, two or three reasons, a closing sentence) is «plan a first draft by generating ideas for writing»; sorting the mixed-up sentences of a piece into opinion, reasons and closing sentence prepares «organizing with structure». The Grade 2 TEKS name no opinion piece of its own (2.12 names literary texts, informational texts and correspondence).

2:draft-an-opinion.why: Writing the piece under Opinion, Reasons and Closing sentence is «organizing with structure»; giving reasons that tell why is «developing an idea with specific and relevant details»; adding a reason or a closing sentence to the draft with a caret after the partner check is «revise drafts by adding, deleting, or rearranging words, phrases, or sentences».

2:friendly-letter.why: Writing a letter with a date, a greeting, a body, a closing and a signature is «compose correspondence such as thank you notes or letters»; choosing "Dear Sam," and "Your friend," among forms with wrong capitals is the «capitalization of ... the salutation and conclusion of a letter»; the printed date with its comma prepares «commas ... in dates».

2:capitals-special-names.why: Telling a name (Lake Erie, Labor Day) from the common word beside it (a lake, a snow day) and writing the name with its capitals is the proper-noun part of «singular, plural, common, and proper nouns»; the Grade 2 capitalization row (2.11.D.ix) names months, days and letters, not holidays and places, so it is not claimed.

3:chapters-scenes-stanzas.why: Finding in which stanza something happens and how a stanza builds on the one before is «structural elements such as stanzas in a variety of poems»; reading a play with a cast, scenes and stage directions and writing a next scene is «elements of drama such as characters, dialogue, setting, and acts»; telling how one chapter builds on the one before prepares «analyze plot elements, including the sequence of events».

3:point-of-view.why: Deciding whether a story is told by a character who says I or by a narrator outside the story, and retelling a part with I and my as another character, is «identify the use of literary devices, including first- or third-person point of view».

3:literal-nonliteral.why: Deciding whether a phrase means just what its words say in this sentence or is a saying with another meaning, and writing that meaning, is the «literal and figurative language» part of «describe how the author's use of imagery, literal and figurative language such as simile, and sound devices ... achieves specific purposes».

3:two-books-one-author.why: Sorting what is true of Story 1, of Story 2 and of both and writing how two stories by one author are alike and different is «synthesize information to create new understanding»; naming each story's lesson, problem, ending and setting in a chart prepares «infer the theme of a work», «analyze plot elements» and «explain the influence of the setting on the plot».

3:two-texts-one-topic.why: Sorting facts as given by Text 1, by Text 2 or by both and writing how the two texts are alike and different is «synthesize information to create new understanding»; choosing each text's most important point apart from its key details is «the central idea with supporting evidence».

1:true-story-plan-and-draft.why: Drawing and noting the three events in the First, Next and Last boxes is «plan a first draft by generating ideas for writing such as by drawing»; writing the true story is «dictate or compose literary texts, including personal narratives»; putting the events in order with First, Next and Last and an ending is «organizing with structure».

1:opinion-and-reason.why: Giving the reason that tells why (matched to its opinion, then written after because) is «developing an idea with specific and relevant details»; writing the topic, the opinion and an ending in order prepares «organizing with structure». The Grade 1 TEKS name no opinion piece of its own (1.12 names literary texts, informational texts and correspondence).

1:all-about-a-topic.why: Writing an All About page with a topic, facts and a closing is «dictate or compose informational texts»; choosing the sentences that are about the topic and writing three facts about it is «developing an idea with specific and relevant details».

1:revise-and-edit-checklist.why: Writing the star sentence again with the detail a partner asked about, and adding that detail to the own draft, is «revise drafts by adding details in pictures or words»; fixing a small letter at the start of a sentence and a small i is «capitalization for the beginning of sentences and the pronoun "I"»; adding the missing end mark is «punctuation marks at the end of declarative, exclamatory, and interrogative sentences».

2:plan-informative-piece.why: Filling the planner (a topic sentence, three facts, a definition, a closing sentence) from a box of facts is «plan a first draft by generating ideas for writing»; sorting facts under two headings and crossing out the sentence that does not belong prepares «organizing with structure».

2:draft-facts-closing.why: Writing the piece from the plan is «compose informational texts, including procedural texts and reports»; keeping the facts of one heading together between a topic sentence and a closing sentence is «organizing with structure»; the facts and the definition of a word are «developing an idea with specific and relevant details».

2:research-class-report.why: Taking notes from two short books to answer the class question is «identify and gather relevant sources and information to answer the questions»; writing the facts in own words under a heading is «demonstrate understanding of information gathered»; the part of the class report is «use an appropriate mode of delivery, whether written, oral, or multimodal, to present results» and a report as 2.12.B names it; marking which book a fact came from and naming both titles prepares «cite sources appropriately». The question is given, so 2.13.A (generate questions) is not claimed.

2:true-story-plan-draft.why: A true story of one small moment is a personal narrative as 2.12.A names it («compose literary texts, including personal narratives and poetry»); the planner (who, where and when, what happened, how I felt) is «plan a first draft by generating ideas for writing»; writing under Beginning, Middle and Ending with time words is «organizing with structure»; the thought, the feeling and the added detail are «developing an idea with specific and relevant details».

2:revise-edit-story.why: Adding a detail with a caret after the partner’s question, crossing out the sentence that does not belong and putting a sentence back in its place are «revise drafts by adding, deleting, or rearranging words, phrases, or sentences»; adding the missing end marks is the «end punctuation» of 2.11.D.x; writing the capital of a name prepares «singular, plural, common, and proper nouns».

2:story-beginning-ending.why: Naming the problem the beginning sets up and how the ending solves it is «describe and understand plot elements, including the main events, the conflict, and the resolution»; telling where the beginning happens prepares «describe the importance of the setting».

2:character-voices.why: Reading a short play with a narrator and three characters is «discuss elements of drama such as characters, dialogue, and setting»; reading each part in a voice that fits is the prosody of «use appropriate fluency rate, accuracy, and prosody when reading grade-level text»; telling what each character thinks prepares «describe the main character’s internal and external traits».

2:two-versions-of-a-tale.why: Two versions of a traditional tale (The Three Little Pigs, The Lion and the Mouse) are «well-known children’s literature such as folktales, fables, and fairy tales»; sorting the facts of both by characters, setting, problem and ending uses the plot elements of 2.8.C, and writing how the versions are alike and different prepares «synthesize information to create new understanding». Texas names no comparison of versions of its own in Grade 2.

2:build-on-others-talk.why: Choosing and writing the reply that builds on a classmate’s comment is «work collaboratively with others by following agreed-upon rules for discussion, including listening to others, speaking when recognized, making appropriate contributions»; staying with the idea under discussion is «share information and ideas that focus on the topic under discussion»; the one thing to say about the book on the talk card prepares «write brief comments on literary or informational texts».

K:opinion-favorite-why.why: Choosing a favorite and drawing it before writing is «plan by generating ideas for writing through class discussions and drawings»; the drawing with its sentence (or the sentence the child tells the teacher) is «develop drafts in oral, pictorial, or written form by organizing ideas». The Kindergarten TEKS name no opinion piece of its own (K.11 names literary and informational texts).

K:fact-draw-label-write.why: Drawing a topic, labeling two parts and writing or telling two facts about it is «dictate or compose informational texts»; the drawing, the labels and the sentences are a draft «in oral, pictorial, or written form».

K:small-moment-draw-write.why: A small moment told in three drawings with a sentence is «dictate or compose literary texts, including personal narratives»; putting the moment in order (first, next, last) is «organizing ideas» in a pictorial and written draft.

K:authors-chair-add-detail.why: Adding the detail a friend asked for is «revise drafts by adding details in pictures or words»; reading the piece from the author’s chair is «share writing»; the friend’s question and the author’s answer are «listen actively and ask questions to understand information and answer questions using multi-word responses».

K:onset-rime-blend.why: Hearing the first sound, then the rest, and circling the picture of the word is «blending spoken onsets and rimes to form simple words». Saying a picture word in its two parts is the step before «segmenting spoken one-syllable words into individual phonemes»; circling the two pictures with the same rest is the identifying half of «identifying and producing rhyming words».

K:two-meanings.why: Hearing a sentence and choosing the picture of the meaning it uses (a bat that flies, a bat for baseball) is «use illustrations and texts the student is able to read or hear to learn or clarify word meanings». Texas first names words with more than one meaning in Grade 3: «use context within and beyond a sentence to determine the meaning of unfamiliar words and multiple-meaning words».

K:compare-two-stories.why: Sorting what happened into Story 1, Story 2, or Both, and telling one more thing both stories tell, is «make connections to personal experiences, ideas in other texts, and society with adult assistance». The cards are the problem, the help, and where the lost thing was found: «describe the elements of plot development, including the main events, the problem, and the resolution for texts read aloud with adult assistance». Circling how each animal felt at the end is «identify and describe the main characters», and drawing what is the same and what is different is «interact with sources in meaningful ways such as illustrating or writing».

1:first-middle-last-sound.why: Texas Grade 1 has no separate expectation for isolating the first, middle, or last sound. Saying each sound of a picture word and touching a box for it is «segmenting spoken one-syllable words of three to five phonemes into individual phonemes, including words with initial and/or final consonant blends»; finding two words that begin with the same sound is «recognizing spoken alliteration or groups of words that begin with the same spoken onset or initial sound». The middle and the last place go one step further than the Texas wording.
